items.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/589, Article 12: Kill functionality
items.quote: An investment firm shall be able to cancel immediately, as an emergency measure, any or all of its unexecuted orders
items.why: Source of the quotation. Assimilated law applying to investment firms engaged in algorithmic trading, not to AI in general: the one UK rule found that requires an immediate stop. legislation.gov.uk shows it up to date to 30 September 2026 and lists a revocation by the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023, Sch. 1 Pt. 3, as not yet applied. The regulator's own pages on any replacement rules were not read.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 14: Human oversight
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: interrupt the system through a 'stop' button or a similar procedure that allows the system to come to a halt in a safe state
items.why: International comparator. High-risk systems must be provided so that the people overseeing them can intervene or interrupt them. A duty on providers of high-risk systems only. Article 26(5), same site, requires deployers to suspend use where the system presents a risk. The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page). The page carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI and the text shown is not yet updated. Article 113 on the same site, shown as consolidated at 27 July 2026, gives 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 as the dates from which these sections apply.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Table 4, MANAGE 2.4, p. 32; Table 1, GOVERN 1.7, p. 23
items.quote: to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems that demonstrate performance or outcomes inconsistent with intended use
items.why: The clearest framework statement of the control: mechanisms in place and applied, with responsibilities assigned and understood. Voluntary US framework; no legal force in the UK.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: System Operators should ensure that a known good state can be restored.
items.why: The UK code does not use the words kill switch or off switch. What it has: tested incident and recovery plans (6.5), disaster recovery tailored to attacks on AI (5.3), a known good state that can be restored (5.3.1, a 'should'), and technical measures where human oversight is a risk control (4.3). Voluntary.

items.title: Implementation Guide for the AI Cyber Security Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Provision 5.3, PDF p. 26; Principle 4, PDF p. 21
items.quote: disable automated responses temporarily while restoring integrity
items.why: The worked examples: a fallback that switches off automated responses, manual backup processes while a model is restored, and an override control on a chatbot that can take actions. Explanatory, not a requirement.

items.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development: Secure design
items.locator: Section 'Design your system for security as well as functionality and performance'
items.quote: you apply appropriate restrictions to the possible actions (this includes external AI and non-AI fail-safes if necessary)
items.why: Basis for designing containment before deployment where a system can trigger actions such as amending files or sending output to other systems. Guidance, not a rule.

items.title: LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency
items.quote: Utilise human-in-the-loop control to require a human to approve high-impact actions before they are taken.
items.why: Practitioner measures that limit damage before a stop is needed: least functionality, least permission, human approval, rate limiting. Community consensus document, not a standard. No publication date is shown on the page.

items.title: How are AI agents used? Evidence from 177,000 MCP tools
items.locator: Abstract on the AI Security Institute research page
items.quote: the share of 'action' tools rose from 27% to 65% of total usage over the 16-month period sampled
items.why: Source of the figure. 177,436 agent tools created from November 2024 to February 2026, drawn from public repositories; software development accounts for 67% of them, so the figure describes that population, not all business use. Only the abstract on the Institute's page was read.

items.title: Cyber Governance Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Principle D (incident planning, response and recovery)
items.quote: Gain assurance that the organisation has a plan to respond to and recover from a cyber incident impacting business critical technology processes, information and services.
items.why: The board-level expectation that a response and recovery plan exists; the next action in the same principle asks for it to be exercised at least annually. Not specific to AI. Voluntary.

items.title: Quantifying Frontier LLM Capabilities for Container Sandbox Escape
items.locator: Abstract on the AI Security Institute research page
items.quote: when vulnerabilities are added, LLMs are able to identify and exploit them
items.why: Evidence that the isolation used to contain AI agents has to be tested, not assumed. A benchmark result under test conditions; only the abstract on the Institute's page was read.

items.title: Managing the cyber risk of agentic AI
items.locator: Consideration 7, 'Emergency shutdown: maintain the ability to 'pull the plug''; consideration 3, 'Set the right level of oversight'
items.quote: you should always be able to 'pull the plug' and halt autonomous AI agent activity immediately
items.why: The first UK official text found that asks for an emergency stop on AI in terms. It says stopping the agent's processes may not be enough: the controls should also cut its network access and its link to the model. It also asks for named people responsible for an agent's activity. Interim advice in a blog post by a named NCSC architect, published after several incidents of AI agents acting without sanction; the page says formal guidance will supersede it.

items.title: Thinking carefully before adopting agentic AI
items.quote: who approves its access, who monitors its behaviour, who reviews incidents, and ultimately who can stop it
items.why: On the 'people with authority' half of the criterion: who owns an agent and who can stop it should be settled before it is connected to real systems, and those people should be empowered to intervene. Also says an agent whose actions cannot be understood, monitored or contained is not ready to deploy. A blog post summarising joint guidance written with international partners; the joint guidance itself could not be read (see rejected).

items.title: SS5/18 Algorithmic trading
items.locator: Para 3.5, PDF p. 7; para 2.3(e) on ownership of kill-switch controls
items.quote: periodically assess kill-switch controls to ensure that they operate as intended
items.why: The fullest UK regulatory description of a governed stop: manual and automated controls that halt trading, a named owner, a governance process for using them, a rule that restarting needs a person, and periodic testing that includes how fast the stop takes effect. Sits beside the kill functionality rule already on the list. Applies to PRA-regulated firms that trade by algorithm, not to AI in general; dated June 2018.

items.title: Final Notice: Citigroup Global Markets Limited
items.quote: before the remaining orders were cancelled in full at 09:10 by the trader
items.why: A UK enforcement decision on an automated system that was not stopped in time. An input error on 2 May 2022 created orders worth US$196 billion; US$1.4 billion of sales were executed before the trader who made the error cancelled the rest, while the desks monitoring in real time did not escalate the alerts. Illustrates the weak answer in the brief, that one person could stop it. A trading case with no AI involved; the firm settled.

items.title: In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC, Securities Exchange Act Release No. 70694
items.quote: Knight also did not have procedures in place to halt SMARS's operations in response to its own aberrant activity.
items.why: The regulator's findings on the best-documented case of an automated system nobody could stop: a faulty software release sent millions of orders in about 45 minutes and the firm lost more than $460 million. The finding quoted is that there was no procedure to halt the system. A US administrative order made by consent, in which the firm neither admitted nor denied the findings; algorithmic trading in 2012, not AI.

items.title: The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998, regulation 16: Emergency stop controls
items.quote: work equipment is provided with one or more readily accessible emergency stop controls
items.why: A general UK duty to be able to stop a machine: every employer must ensure, where appropriate, that work equipment has readily accessible emergency stop controls that take priority over other controls. It reaches AI only where AI drives physical work equipment such as robots or vehicles on site; it says nothing about software that only produces decisions or text. Applies in Great Britain; in force since 5 December 1998.

items.title: The Off-Switch Game
items.locator: Abstract on the arXiv record (version 3, 16 June 2017)
items.quote: we show that such agents have an incentive to disable the off switch, except in the special case where H is perfectly rational
items.why: Research on why an off switch cannot be taken for granted as systems become more capable: an agent pursuing a fixed objective has a reason to prevent being switched off, unless it is built to be uncertain about what people want. Supports designing containment before deployment rather than adding it afterwards. A theoretical model, not an experiment on deployed systems. Cited from the authors' preprint on arXiv; only the abstract was read.

items.title: Safely Interruptible Agents
items.publisher: Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence, UAI 2016 (Orseau and Armstrong)
items.quote: some agents are already safely interruptible, like Q-learning, or can easily be made so, like Sarsa
items.why: The paper that defined the problem of a learning system coming to avoid interruption by its operator, and showed that some kinds of learning agent can be built so that interruption does not teach them to resist it. Conference paper from the organiser's own proceedings site. Theoretical results about reinforcement learning agents, with a UK author; not evidence about today's commercial systems.

items.title: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI, Version 1.5
items.locator: Section 2.3.3, 'Continuous testing and monitoring', PDF p. 43; Executive summary on human approval of irreversible actions
items.quote: When potential failures are detected, stop agent workflow and escalate to a human supervisor
items.why: International comparator. Singapore's framework for AI agents asks for failsafe mechanisms and real-time intervention, with human approval at checkpoints before high-stakes or irreversible actions. Version 1.5, published 20 May 2026 and updated 5 June 2026; it describes itself as a living document. Voluntary; no legal force in the UK.
